title: 📅 Project Management Mastery — The Atlas Migration
subtitle: Run a 90-day enterprise platform migration end-to-end — schedule, scope, risk, people
theme: First-time PM running a high-stakes enterprise migration with a real critical path
description: You are the newly appointed Project Manager for the 'Atlas Migration' — moving Atlas Corp's flagship customer platform from a legacy monolith to a new microservices architecture. Budget: $1.8M. Team: 14 people across engineering, design, QA, and ops. Hard deadline: Day 90 (linked to a regulatory cutover). Six rounds across kickoff, sprint planning, mid-project crisis, scope creep, vendor delay, and the launch decision. You'll author OKRs, run a RAID register, and defend your critical path.
learning_objectives: Identify and defend the critical path through forward and backward DAG passes
Run a RAID register (Risks/Assumptions/Issues/Dependencies) as a living artifact, not a deck slide
Make calibrated trade-offs between scope, schedule, cost, and quality under pressure
Communicate schedule slippage to executive sponsors before they ask
Decide when to crash the schedule, fast-track tasks, or descope ruthlessly

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each round advances the project clock by 1-3 weeks. Read the project dashboard: critical path, burndown, RAID, sprint state.
Pick the option that protects the critical path while honoring the iron triangle (scope/schedule/cost).
Author your OKRs, RAID checkpoint, and post-mortem when prompted.
Watch the schedule_health pill — once it slips to 'at_risk' you have one round to recover.
tips: Tasks not on the critical path have float — slip them deliberately, not by accident.
A RAID risk you don't write down is one your sponsor will surface in front of the steering committee.
Crashing (adding people) costs money and slows the team for ~1 sprint. Fast-tracking (parallelizing) creates rework.
The deadline you tell your team should be 1 sprint earlier than the deadline you tell your sponsor.

target_audience: Accelerator/MBA/PMP/CSM students, first-time PMs, engineering leads moving into delivery roles

psychological_framework.description: PM dimensions: critical-path thinking, risk management, scope discipline, stakeholder communication, decision quality, team leadership.

hallmarks: Authors outcome-based OKRs in Sprint 1 — not output checklists
Defends the critical path with explicit forward/backward DAG passes
Treats RAID as a living artifact, not a deck slide
Pre-empts sponsor escalations — a brief in week 3 beats a panic in week 6

competitor_ai.context: Three peer firms running parallel enterprise migrations under the same regulatory cutover. Their moves react to your decision_panel commits.

rounds.title: Sprint 1 — Kickoff & OKRs
rounds.scenario: Day 1. You inherit a charter that says 'go-live by Day 90'. The CTO wants OKRs by end of week. The team is anxious — three of them survived the failed migration attempt 18 months ago. You have one shot to set the bar without overcommitting.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Project manager standing at a whiteboard with OKR sticky notes, diverse engineering team seated around table

choices.label: Author outcome-based OKRs (e.g., 'Cut customer-reported defects 60% in hypercare') and publish them.
choices.feedback: CTO loved the customer-outcome framing. Tech Lead Priya volunteered to own KR2 herself.

decision_record.rationale: Outcome OKRs anchor scope discussions later

choices.expert_rationale: Outcome-based OKRs ('cut customer-reported defects 60% in hypercare') anchor the team to what users feel — not what engineers ship. This single decision is the highest-leverage move in the entire project.

choices.label: Author output-based OKRs ('Ship 12 services', 'Migrate 4 schemas') — easy to track.
choices.feedback: OKRs read like a project plan. CTO asked, 'What's the customer outcome?' You didn't have it.

decision_record.rationale: Outputs are easier to track but harder to defend

choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'Ship 12 services' is easy to track and easy to game. It's also easy to hit while customers churn.

choices.label: Skip OKRs for now — 'we'll know what success looks like by Sprint 3'.
choices.feedback: Three weeks later the COO asked, 'How do we know if this is working?' You had no answer.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'We'll know it when we see it' is what teams say in Sprint 1 and regret in Sprint 5 when they're arguing about scope.

decision_panel.title: Sprint 1 — Operating Cadence
decision_panel.subtitle: Set the rhythm before you set the scope. These four levers shape every decision in Rounds 2-6.

controls.label: Sprint length (days)
controls.description: Industry default is 14 days. Shorter = faster feedback but more ceremony overhead.

controls.label: Number of OKRs
controls.description: Doerr's rule: > 5 OKRs and none of them count.

controls.label: Schedule contingency buffer
controls.description: PMI standard for novel architecture work is 15-20%.

controls.label: Sponsor comms cadence
controls.description: Pre-emptive comms is the #1 PMI predictor of project survival.

expert_debrief.title: Why we'd lean into outcome OKRs and a 15% schedule buffer
expert_debrief.body: Three decisions in Sprint 1 set the trajectory for the entire 90-day cutover. First, outcome-based OKRs ('cut customer-reported defects 60% in hypercare') anchor every downstream scope discussion to what users feel — not what engineers ship. Second, a 15% contingency on a 90-day regulatory cutover is the standard PMI buffer for unfamiliar architecture work; less than 10% and you'll be fighting fires by Sprint 4. Third, weekly sponsor comms costs you 30 minutes and buys you the right to deliver bad news before someone else does — PMI's #1 predictor of project survival. Three OKRs (not six) keeps team attention finite. Doerr's rule: more than five OKRs means none of them count.

citations.label: Project Management Institute Pulse of the Profession 2023

rounds.title: Sprint 2 — The Critical Path Reveal
rounds.scenario: Day 14. Discovery finished. The DAG pass shows your true critical path runs kickoff → discovery → arch_design → build_core → data_migration → cutover_rehearse → go_live → hypercare = 79 days. You have 11 days of float total. Priya asks: 'Should we crash arch_design with two more architects?'
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Engineering team gathered around a wall-sized DAG diagram with the critical path highlighted in red

choices.label: Fast-track arch_design — start build_core stubs in parallel, accept ~15% rework risk.
choices.feedback: Parallelism cut design wall-clock by 4 days. Priya flagged ~3 weeks of rework risk in build_core if design pivots.

add.label: Build rework risk from parallel design (~3w)

decision_record.rationale: Fast-tracking trades quality risk for schedule

choices.expert_rationale: Fast-tracking arch_design with parallel build_core stubs accepts ~15% rework in exchange for ~14 days of float. Calculated risk + explicit RAID entry = professional PM.

choices.label: Crash the schedule — hire 2 architects from the agency at $30K/week.
choices.feedback: Cost +$120K. Brooks's Law: ramp-up cost meant only 2 days saved. Burned 7% of budget.

decision_record.rationale: Crashing is expensive on knowledge work

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Hiring 2 architects at $30K/week is the textbook example of crashing a schedule too late — Brooks's Law says you'll lose more than you gain.

choices.label: Keep design serial — protect quality, eat the schedule slack.
choices.feedback: Clean handoff to build, but you've used 9 of your 11 float days before Sprint 3 begins.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Serial design protects quality but eats every day of your float. Schedule risk is irreversible; rework risk is recoverable.

decision_panel.title: Sprint 2 — Critical Path Levers
decision_panel.subtitle: 11 days of float, 79-day critical path. Choose what to spend, where, and when to freeze design.

controls.label: Build_core parallel-start overlap
controls.description: % of build_core stubs to start before arch_design freezes.

controls.label: Accepted rework risk budget
controls.description: Calibrated upper bound. Above 20% and you're recklessly parallel.

controls.label: Design freeze gate (project day)
controls.description: Day at which arch_design is locked to enable build_core scaling.

controls.label: Architects on the build
controls.description: Brooks's Law lurks above 3 on a 90-day knowledge-work project.

expert_debrief.title: Why we'd fast-track 30% — not crash, not stay serial
expert_debrief.body: The critical path has 79 days of work and you have 11 days of float — that's a 12% buffer on a regulatory-locked deadline, which is below what PMI calls the 'safe corridor' for novel architecture work. Fast-tracking 30% of build_core stubs in parallel buys back ~14 days of schedule float in exchange for a ~15% rework probability — a defensible asymmetric trade. Crashing the schedule by hiring two architects is the textbook violation of Brooks's Law: ramp-up cost on knowledge work means you'll pay $120K and recover only 2 days. Staying serial is the most expensive choice — it eats 9 of your 11 float days before Sprint 3, leaving you no buffer for the vendor delay coming in Round 3 (which the RAID register already flagged).
expert_debrief.expert_voice: Frederick Brooks, Mythical Man-Month + PMI Practice Standard for Scheduling

citations.label: PMI Practice Standard for Scheduling, 2nd Ed

rounds.title: Sprint 3 — Vendor Slip
rounds.scenario: Day 28. DataMesh emails: their cutover SDK will be 3 weeks late — landing Day 65 instead of Day 44. This was a known risk (r_vendor). Build_integrations sits behind it on the DAG. Your move.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Project manager on phone in a war room with a Gantt chart showing a red delay bar, team watching

choices.label: Build an internal SDK stub now; integrate the real one when it lands.
choices.feedback: Stub took 8 days. Build_integrations could proceed. Real SDK swap-in in Sprint 5 was clean.

forecast_capture.question: Forecast vendor slip duration in business days. Provide an 80% CI (e.g. 5 to 18)

forecast_prompt.question: Forecast vendor slip duration in business days. Provide an 80% CI (e.g. 5 to 18). Narrower = more credit if covered.

choices.expert_rationale: An internal SDK stub creates an integration boundary you control. When DataMesh ships, you swap implementations behind the boundary. When they slip again, you don't slip.

choices.label: Wait for DataMesh — escalate to the COO to lean on their CEO.
choices.feedback: COO called. Vendor pulled in by 1 week. You still lost 14 days off the critical path.

add.label: Vendor slip ate 14 days of float

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Escalating to the COO doesn't change DataMesh's schedule — it just creates a political artifact for your status report.

choices.label: Descope the vendor integration to Phase 2 — go-live without it.
choices.feedback: Compliance lead Lin escalated: the vendor integration is in the regulatory cutover scope.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Descoping the vendor integration to Phase 2 violates the compliance gate. The audit team finds it during pre-prod and you're back in week-3 negotiations in week 8.

decision_panel.title: Sprint 3 — Vendor Risk Response
decision_panel.subtitle: DataMesh slipped 3 weeks. The dependency was on the critical path. Choose your hedge.

controls.label: Days to invest in internal SDK stub
controls.description: Enough to unblock build_integrations without competing with vendor's real SDK.

controls.label: Vendor escalation level
controls.description: Too low = ignored. Too high = relationship damage.

controls.label: Keep vendor track live in parallel?
controls.description: Dual-track de-risking: build internal stub AND keep vendor integration warm.

controls.label: RAID review cadence
controls.description: How often you re-walk the risk register. Stale RAID = surprise crisis.

expert_debrief.title: Why we'd dual-track: build the stub AND keep the vendor warm
expert_debrief.body: The vendor delay was a known risk on your RAID register — the test isn't whether you saw it coming, it's whether your mitigation was pre-positioned. An internal stub at 8 days is a calibrated investment: enough to unblock build_integrations without becoming a parallel product. Keeping the vendor track live in parallel is the dual-track move HBR cases call 'optionality preservation' — you're not betting against the vendor, you're insuring against their slip. Descoping the integration to Phase 2 trades a known short-term cost for an unknown long-term one (technical debt, customer-feature gap). Waiting for the vendor with no stub is the failure mode the RAID register exists to prevent — you logged the risk and then behaved as if it wouldn't happen.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: HBR — 'Vendor Risk Management for the Modern PM' (paraphrased)

citations.label: HBR — Real Options in Project Risk Management

rounds.title: Sprint 4 — The Scope Creep Conversation
rounds.scenario: Day 42. The COO 'casually' adds two requirements: a new analytics dashboard, and SSO support for an acquired subsidiary. Each is ~10 days of work. Your team is at 92% capacity. Your sponsor is the CTO (who'd say no), but the COO outranks her.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Tense meeting with executive pointing at slide showing new feature requests, PM holding up scope-change form

choices.label: Write a scope-change memo — 'Adding these = +15 days OR drop hypercare. Pick.'
choices.feedback: COO blinked. Both items moved to Phase 2. CTO was thrilled you held the line.

decision_record.rationale: Surfaced trade-off in writing — forced an executive decision

choices.expert_rationale: A written scope-change memo with the iron-triangle framing forces the sponsor to choose. PMs who don't write the memo end up absorbing the work and missing the date anyway.

choices.label: Absorb the work quietly — push the team to '110%' for two sprints.
choices.feedback: Team morale dropped from 75 to 50. Two engineers took mental health days. SSO integration was buggy.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Pushing a team to 110% for two sprints destroys morale and creates the bug pile that explodes during UAT.

choices.label: Offer a swap: take SSO (10d), defer analytics — but only if hypercare gets full team attention.
choices.feedback: Reasonable trade. COO accepted. SSO landed clean. Analytics shipped 60 days post-launch.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Trading SSO for analytics + full hypercare protection sounds clever but adds a learning curve mid-sprint. Don't run multi-variable trades without a freeze.

inbox_events.subject: Can we add SSO to v1?
inbox_events.body: Big enterprise prospect needs SSO before signing. Add it now or in v1.1?

choices.label: Hold the line — SSO is v1.1
Add SSO — re-baseline schedule

decision_panel.title: Sprint 4 — Scope-Schedule-Cost Triangle
decision_panel.subtitle: Two new asks at 92% utilization. Set the iron triangle now or watch your team burn.

controls.label: New scope to absorb without renegotiation
controls.description: Above 0 means absorbing the COO's asks silently. Sustainability ceiling: 0.

controls.label: Target team utilization
controls.description: 85% is the sustainable ceiling on knowledge work. Above 95% = burnout in 2 sprints.

controls.label: Slip days before sponsor escalation
controls.description: Pre-emptive disclosure beats reactive damage control.

controls.label: Offer feature swap?
controls.description: Swap proposes a trade. Memo presents the trade-off. Both honor the iron triangle.

expert_debrief.title: Why we'd write the scope-change memo before swapping anything
expert_debrief.body: Scope creep at 92% utilization is not a scope problem — it's a renegotiation problem. The scope-change memo is the explicit move HBR teaches: surface the iron triangle ('+15 days OR drop hypercare — pick'), force the COO to own the trade-off, and create the paper trail your team needs to operate at sustainable pace. Absorbing the work quietly is the failure mode McKinsey research links to a 3x burnout rate and a 40% drop in defect quality by Sprint 6 — you don't save schedule, you trade it for downstream rework. Offering a swap (SSO for analytics) is tactically clever but strategically wrong here: it concedes the principle that scope is negotiable on the COO's terms. Memo first, swap second only if memo gets dismissed.

citations.label: HBR — Saying No to Your Sponsor
McKinsey — Sustainable Pace in Knowledge Work, 2022

rounds.title: Sprint 5 — UAT Crisis
rounds.scenario: Day 70. UAT failed: 12 critical defects, 4 of which are in vendor integration. Schedule_health flipped to 'slipping'. Marco (QA) wants to delay go-live by 2 weeks. The CTO is asking for a recovery plan by Friday. Your hypercare buffer is gone.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: QA team and engineers reviewing red defect dashboard, project manager building recovery slide on laptop

choices.label: Triage by severity, freeze new work, run fix-and-retest sprints. Communicate 1-week slip to sponsor.
choices.feedback: Disciplined recovery. 11 of 12 defects closed in 9 days. CTO appreciated the early signal.

add.label: 12 critical UAT defects — recovery plan active

decision_record.rationale: Pre-emptive sponsor brief is the highest-leverage PM move

choices.expert_rationale: Triage by severity, freeze new work, fix-and-retest sprints, weekly comms to sponsor. This is exactly what a PMP-grade PM does in a UAT crisis.

choices.label: Ship on time with known issues — log them, fix in hypercare.
choices.feedback: Compliance lead Lin blocked go-live. Two of the defects were regulatory. You went past Day 90 anyway.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Shipping with 12 critical defects logged 'for hypercare' is how go-lives become rollbacks 36 hours later. Customers don't read your bug log.

choices.label: Take the full 2-week delay Marco wants — clean go-live or no go-live.
choices.feedback: Quality protected. CTO accepted. COO grumbled — 2 weeks is the gap before the regulatory window closes.

decision_record.rationale: Schedule slip is recoverable, regulatory miss is not

choices.counterfactual_feedback: A clean 2-week delay is sometimes right — but only if your sponsor map is aligned. At week 5 with no pre-emptive brief, this becomes a no-confidence event.

decision_panel.title: Sprint 5 — Recovery Posture
decision_panel.subtitle: 12 critical defects, schedule slipping, sponsor wants a plan Friday. Calibrate the recovery.

controls.label: Days between learning bad news and disclosing to sponsor
controls.description: Kerzner: every day of lag doubles the political cost of disclosure.

controls.label: Critical defects acceptable at go-live
controls.description: Zero is not aspirational — it's the contract for a regulatory cutover.

controls.label: Hypercare team headcount
controls.description: Too small = oncall burnout. Too large = build team starves.

controls.label: Fix-and-retest sprints before go-live
controls.description: Each sprint adds 1 week schedule but ~3x defect kill rate.

expert_debrief.title: Why we'd take the 1-week slip — not ship dirty, not delay 2
expert_debrief.body: UAT failure with 12 critical defects on a regulatory-locked cutover is the moment Kerzner's 'Project Recovery' framework was written for. Three rules apply: First, disclose to the sponsor within 24 hours — every additional day of lag doubles the political cost (Kerzner's empirical finding across 600 troubled projects). Second, 0 critical defects at go-live is non-negotiable for a regulatory cutover; the 'ship dirty, fix in hypercare' choice costs 3-5x more in customer trust than a 1-week slip. Third, structured recovery — triage, freeze, fix-and-retest — is the only posture that compresses defect-kill cadence from typical 1.2x/sprint to ~3x/sprint. The 2-week delay Marco wants is over-correction: it preserves quality but costs you sponsor credibility for the rest of hypercare and beyond.

citations.label: PMI — Pulse of the Profession 2024 (recovery patterns)

rounds.title: Sprint 6 — The Go-Live Call
rounds.scenario: Day 84. Cutover rehearsal: 1 minor issue (rollback script fails on edge case affecting 0.3% of customers). Compliance audit: clean. Vendor SDK: integrated. Team morale: 65% (recovered from r4). You're chairing the go/no-go call tomorrow.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Project manager at a podium in a packed war room, big screen showing go/no-go checklist

choices.label: GO. Manual workaround for 0.3% edge case, runbook to ops, hypercare hot-fix in week 1.
choices.feedback: Cutover succeeded. Edge case hit 6 customers; ops handled it cleanly. CTO promoted you to Senior PM.

decision_record.rationale: Reversible go-live with documented workaround beats endless polish

choices.expert_rationale: GO with a documented manual workaround for the 0.3% edge case + runbook + week-2 hot-fix is the calibrated answer. Real PMs ship; they don't chase zero-defect ghosts.

choices.label: NO-GO. Delay 1 week for a perfect rollback script.
choices.feedback: Defensible but expensive. Regulatory window narrowed to 2 days. Team morale dropped 10%.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A perfect rollback script for a 0.3% edge case is what PMs ask for when they're scared, not when they're running the math. The cost of delay > the cost of the workaround.

choices.label: GO with no workaround — hot-fix in production if it triggers.
choices.feedback: Cutover hit 6 customers with a hard error. Two churned. Press release to compliance was painful.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: GO with no workaround because 'we'll hot-fix in production' is how data gets lost during the cutover window. The runbook isn't optional.

decision_panel.title: Sprint 6 — Go/No-Go Decision Posture
decision_panel.subtitle: 1 minor edge case, 0.3% blast radius. Calibrate the rollback envelope and oncall posture.

controls.label: Rollback decision window during cutover
controls.description: Time-boxed go/no-go reassessment after cutover starts.

controls.label: Workaround runbook depth
controls.description: Ops needs enough to execute under pressure. Too long = nobody reads it.

controls.label: Hypercare oncall team size (week 1)
controls.description: Week 1 oncall is 50% triage, 50% pattern recognition.

controls.label: Go/no-go quorum threshold
controls.description: % of voting members required for GO. ITIL Major Change recommends ≥80%.

expert_debrief.title: Why we'd GO with a workaround — not chase zero-defect perfection
expert_debrief.body: 0.3% blast radius with a documented workaround is the textbook GO posture in ITIL Major Change Management. Three calibrations make this responsible: First, a 15-minute rollback decision window is the discipline that prevents 'sunk cost' GO calls — if reality diverges from runbook in the first 15 min, you reverse without ego. Second, a 6-page runbook is the McKinsey-validated sweet spot for ops execution under pressure (10+ pages = unread; 1-2 pages = under-specified). Third, an 80% quorum threshold means the call has consensus authority, not pluralities. Delaying for a perfect rollback script (NO-GO) is the failure mode every change-management textbook warns against: it converts a managed 0.3% risk into an unmanaged sponsor-credibility loss. Going without a workaround trades known risk for unknown — exactly the opposite of what mature PM discipline trains for.
expert_debrief.expert_voice: ITIL 4 Major Change Management + McKinsey Cutover Playbook (paraphrased)

platinum.label: PMP-grade delivery
platinum.description: Critical path defended, RAID stayed live, sponsors briefed pre-emptively, calibrated trade-offs throughout. You'd be hired into a Senior PM role tomorrow.

gold.label: Strong PM
gold.description: Solid delivery with minor scope/communication misses. You belong in the role; sharpen pre-emptive sponsor briefs.

silver.label: Capable PM
silver.description: Got it shipped but with avoidable rework. Re-read your RAID — what would you have surfaced earlier?

bronze.label: Apprentice PM
bronze.description: Project shipped (or didn't) more on luck than discipline. Re-run with a real critical-path defense in Round 2.

glossary_terms.definition: Longest dependency chain in a project DAG; slipping any task on it slips the whole project.
Days a non-critical task can slip without delaying the project.
Adding resources to shorten a task — costs money, often hits Brooks's Law on knowledge work.
Running tasks in parallel that were planned serial — risks rework if upstream pivots.
Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies — the living register of project unknowns.
Cumulative completed-work vs total-work over time; the slope tells you if you'll land.
Scope/Schedule/Cost (with Quality at the center) — pick which two to fix.
User Acceptance Testing — the last gate before production cutover.
Heightened-support window post-launch — on-call rotation, fast triage, rollback ready.
Final cutover decision — chaired by PM, attended by sponsors, QA, ops, compliance.

reflection_prompts: Which decision moved the schedule_health pill the most — yours or the vendor's?
What did your RAID register catch in Round 3 that would have blindsided you otherwise?
When did you choose schedule over scope, and would you make the same trade-off again?
coaching_moment: The single highest-leverage PM move is the pre-emptive sponsor brief. If your sponsor learns about a slip from anyone but you, you've already lost. Round 5 was the test — and if you took the structured recovery path, you passed it.
